newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African banks hike short-term money mkt rates.
newsitem.headline: S.African banks hike short-term money mkt rates.

text.p: South Africa's "big four" banks hiked their short-term deposit rates by 10 basis points on Monday, their first movement in over a month, dealers said.
At the same time, forward rates extended their recent decline, falling to fresh six-and-a-half month lows.

Three-month NCDs were quoted at between 15.55 and 15.65 percent offered, up from 15.55 percent on Friday as similar dated rand forward prices fell to 11.20 bid -- their lowest level since September last year.
Money market traders said that rates had been adjusted on screen to reflect where they had been trading over the last week.
"The market has been trading off the screens at those levels...there is nothing sinister in the move," a senior trader said. "We are just adjusting to where the actual level of rates is."
"There has been quite a lot of trade happening at this sort of level for the last week and people haven't been updating their screens. I wouldn't read too much into it," another senior trader said.
Forward traders said rates had come off as the local market was discounting a further U.S. interest rate hike at the Federal Reserve's next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on May 20.
In a pre-emptive strike against a possible rise in U.S. inflation, the Fed hiked interest rates by 25 basis points on March 25.

However, further signs of inflationary pressures, most recently in March average hourly earnings which showed a four percent year-on-year rise, have boosted speculation of a further tightening next month.
"The U.S. are talking another rate hike at the next meeting, so the forwards are coming off," a trader said.
"(The forwards) are under differentials already so they are discounting a further 25 point hike when the Fed meets again on May 20," he said.

Traders said that while the two markets were giving conflicting signs on local interest rates, no movement was expected in the foreseeable future, particularly after worse-than-expected credit extension figures last week.

Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals has cited private sector credit extension, which rose 17.34 percent year-on-year in February from 17.06 percent in January, as one of the main indicators which will have to be reduced before he considers a rate cut.
Bank rate, which currently stands at 17 percent, was last hiked by one percentage point on November 21 last year.
